Limitation: the retrievable text gives the process change and the accuracy anecdotes but no effect size on minutes, and the 18-developer study is the kind of evidence that gets cited as 'faster' without a number attached; the paper was CLOSED access via Semantic Scholar and both the NSF PAR and IEEE PDFs failed to fetch, so the per-task timing table could not be checked. This is the node most likely to be wrong in a favourable direction.

nodes.title: Queued humans approve in seconds, so checkpoint minutes measure queue clearing, not review
nodes.body: Practitioner instrumentation reports are consistent on the order of magnitude: one operations analyst facing a 383-item agent queue had a median review of nine seconds (open, glance, approve), declining two items in four hours; another author reports approval logs where blocked proposals averaged 94 seconds of review while the 56 approved ones averaged 23 seconds, and the four that caused post-approval incidents were each under 8 seconds. The same sources propose the detector that matters: compare approval latency against diff size and watch zero-comment approvals on non-trivial changes, and seed 1-2% known-bad items to measure the rubber stamp directly. The mechanism is that a queue transfers cost from judgement to throughput: the human optimises for clearing, and the cheapest action that keeps the queue moving is approval, so measured minutes per checkpoint fall as the number of checkpoints rises, which is exactly backwards from what an oversight metric should reward. Limitation: these are blog-post anecdotes with no published dataset, no sampling frame and no code, they are self-selected and possibly dramatised, and they are about refund and credit-line approval rather than code; the honest reading is that the order of magnitude is plausible and corroborated by the wave-2 rubber-stamp result (97% per-action approval), not that nine seconds is a code-review constant.

nodes.title: An RCT found experienced maintainers 19% slower with AI, review eating the savings
nodes.body: METR's randomized controlled trial (Feb-June 2025) had 16 experienced open-source maintainers complete 246 real issues from their own repositories, randomly assigned to AI-assisted or unassisted; AI-assisted tasks took 19% longer, while the developers had predicted a 24% speedup beforehand and still believed afterwards that AI had helped. The mechanism is compositional: time shifted into writing prompts and into reviewing and reworking generated output, and the saving on typing was smaller than the added review and rework, which is the same accounting problem loom has, since every attempt it produces becomes human review surface unless the verifier can reject it autonomously. Limitation: n=16, a very experienced and unusually fast population on mature repositories with high context cost, a 2025 tool set, and a 19% figure with a wide interval; it does not say the review share specifically grew, only that the total got worse. Its value here is as the adversarial counterweight to any claim that agent throughput converts into human minutes saved.

nodes.title: Re-entry after an interruption costs ~23 minutes, dwarfing a 3.5-minute decision
nodes.body: Gloria Mark's workplace studies (UC Irvine) put the cost of returning to a suspended task after an interruption at roughly 23 minutes 15 seconds, and report that knowledge workers switch tasks about every three minutes. Arithmetic that matters for loom: if a checkpoint interrupts the human rather than waiting in a queue, one approval costs about one decision interval (3.5 minutes in the SAFE study, 13-14 minutes for a 100-line change in di Biase) plus up to 23 minutes of re-entry for whatever they were doing, so the human-minute denominator is dominated by the interruption, not by the review. The mechanism is that resumption requires rebuilding the suspended task's working memory, and that reconstruction is priced in minutes regardless of how small the interrupting decision was. Limitation: the 23-minute figure is a synthesis of observational field studies of office knowledge work, not a controlled measurement of code review, it predates agent tooling, and the underlying construct (what counts as returning to the task) is contested; a well-designed async checkpoint with batched questions could pay the re-entry cost once per batch instead of once per decision, which is the design implication rather than a fixed penalty.

nodes.title: 14% of review comments concern defects and 75% found are evolvability, not behaviour
nodes.body: Bacchelli & Bird (ICSE 2013, Microsoft) classified 570 comments across about 200 reviews and found the most frequent outcome to be code improvements at 29%, with defect finding at 14%, while reviewers themselves named understanding the change and its rationale as the main challenge and were observed to spend effort on easy stylistic issues while missing serious ones. Mäntylä & Lassenius (IEEE TSE 2009) found 75% of defects found in review do not affect visible functionality, i.e. they are evolvability defects, and Beller et al.'s taxonomy work reports the remaining functional share at roughly 15%. The mechanism is that review is primarily a comprehension and design-communication activity, and defect detection is a by-product of the comprehension; a metric that scores only observable-behaviour defects prices the minority output and ignores the majority. Limitation: the comment taxonomy is from Microsoft's C# workflow in 2012-2013, the 14% figure depends on how 'defect' is operationalised, and evolvability defects are exactly the kind our shell verifier cannot see, which cuts both ways: it means a verifier-scored gate will systematically under-price what the human caught, but it also means the human's contribution is not measurable by any automated score we could put in the numerator.

nodes.title: AI PRs wait 4.6x longer for pickup while their reviews run faster once started
nodes.body: LinearB's 2026 benchmark dataset, as summarised by prlens.dev from 8.1M PRs, reports AI-assisted PRs at 408 lines at the 75th percentile versus 157 unassisted, AI-generated PRs waiting 4.6x longer for pickup (over 16 hours versus about 200 minutes) while the review itself runs faster once started (~194 minutes versus ~252 minutes). Both quantities are time-in-state, so this is not a minutes measurement, but the pickup/review split is the decomposition a checkpoint design has to respect: bigger machine-written changes lose their time in the queue, where nobody is being helped, and only the second interval converts into human attention. The mechanism is triage economics: a reviewer facing an unfamiliar 400-line machine-authored diff defers it in favour of a change whose risk they can estimate in a glance, so queue time absorbs the cost of the agent's volume. Limitation: vendor benchmark data with an undisclosed vendor-specific methodology, AI-authored and AI-assisted defined by heuristics, no causal identification, and the 'review runs faster' side could be entirely the ESEM 2026 centrality confound described above.

nodes.title: The only defensible denominator is instrumented open-to-verdict time per checkpoint
nodes.body: Given the above, human-minutes for loom should be defined operationally rather than borrowed: start the clock when the human first opens the checkpoint artefact (diff, failing test output, paired baseline), stop it at the first stated verdict action (approve, reject, edit), exclude time the artefact was open in a background tab, and report the excluded queue interval separately as a second number. This is exactly the construction the SAFE study had to reconstruct from transcripts after the fact (median 3.5 min per finding), and exactly what Meta's TimeSpent approximates for diffs, so it has precedent but no standard. The mechanism is that the two components have different optima: queue minutes are bought down by batching and assignment, active minutes by packaging and by not showing the reviewer work they did not ask for (the Meta AI-patch collapse), and a single blended number lets a design score well by destroying the queue while leaving the review untouched. Limitation: first-open-to-verdict still includes re-reading and page-turning, background-tab exclusion is a heuristic, and per-checkpoint medians of 3.5 to 14 minutes mean a headline metric over a handful of checkpoints per round has enormous sampling error, so any per-round gain of 0.05 in a 0-1 score is likely to be inside the noise of its own denominator.

nodes.title: Windows rename over an open file failed 1500 of 1691 times (88%): EPERM, not a rare race
nodes.body: loom publishes every derived file with writeFileSync(tmp) then renameSync(target) (`src/core/atomic.js:13-18`). I ran three reader processes calling readFileSync in a tight loop on the same path while one writer republished it every iteration. In a temp dir 1500 of 1691 renames failed; the same loop rooted at C:/Projects/RSI failed 1737 of 1968; error code was EPERM (errno -4048) every time and no reader ever saw a torn value. The identical loop with no readers did 1990/1990 and 2075/2075. Here the mechanism is that MoveFileEx honours sharing modes: a reader that opened without FILE_SHARE_DELETE makes the replace fail immediately instead of waiting, so the collision is the common case whenever the panel, a second window, an editor or Defender touches the same file, not a rare race. Why this matters for restart safety: the lease and the lock are written through this same primitive, so the one write that must succeed before dispatch is the one most able to fail. Limitation: my readers used plain readFileSync, which does not request FILE_SHARE_DELETE; a cooperating reader that did would not collide, so this bounds the risk from node-style readers, not from every process on Windows.

nodes.title: writeJsonAtomic has no retry, no fsync, and leaks the temp file on every failed rename
nodes.body: `src/core/atomic.js:13-18` is `writeFileSync(tmp,...); renameSync(tmp,path)` with no catch, no backoff and no cleanup, and `writeOwnership` in `src/core/lock.js:28-32` is the same shape. Under the three-reader load, 777 orphan `*.tmp` files accumulated in two seconds, because the temp write succeeds and only the rename fails, so a failed publish is also a disk leak that nothing sweeps (lease sweeping in `src/runtime/lease.js:95-109` covers leases only). Separately, a grep for fsync/fdatasync/flushSync across src returns nothing: even a successful rename publishes name-before-data, so the directory entry can be durable while the content is not. Windows has no POSIX directory-fsync guarantee, and NTFS's metadata journaling covers the rename, not the file body. Here the mechanism is that atomicity of the name and durability of the bytes are different properties, and the code has only the first. Limitation: on a workstation the realistic loss window is a hard power cut, not a process kill, so this is a durability defect rather than a daily failure; and a failed publish that throws simply crashes that one round, which the restart path is designed to absorb.

nodes.title: 4200 appends under the same reader load: zero failures while rename failed 88%
nodes.body: appendJsonl (`src/core/atomic.js:20-33`) never asks Windows to move a name over an open handle, and it showed 4200/4200 successes with three tight-loop readers running against the same directory, measured in the same process that was failing renames. Here the mechanism is that append opens with append access and an existing reader's share mode does not forbid extending the file, whereas rename additionally needs DELETE access on the destination, which is exactly what a plain reader denies. This makes the architecture's own choice defensible in a way the code does not state: the append-only ledger is the durable, crash-tolerant part, and the snapshot files (views/state.json, leases/*.json, lock) are the fragile part, because they are the only things that replace a name. Consequence for restart safety: a lease that cannot be written is not a lease, so hardening should move leases onto the append path and derive current state by folding, rather than trying to make rename reliable. Limitation: append is safe against concurrent readers but not against a torn write from a killed writer, which is why the manual newline prefix and the torn-line skip exist; append of a record larger than one write is not atomic, so safety here is per-line and the code has to repair the seam.

nodes.title: The standard 12-retry backoff fix managed 7 publishes in 2 s and still failed twice
nodes.body: The widely copied remedy for EPERM-on-rename is a retry loop (12 attempts, backoff capped at 100 ms, about 0.6 s of patience), which is what claude-hooks and gortex adopted after the same failure. I implemented exactly that against the same three-reader load: 7 successful publishes, 2 hard failures after exhausting all attempts, and 60 rename attempts spent in two seconds, against 151 successes for a plain single-shot rename in the same interval. Here the mechanism is that the readers are continuously reopening the file, so backoff never creates a gap wide enough to win; the retry converts a fast failure into a slow one and pushes a publish's latency toward its patience budget. For a loop that ticks every 20 s and writes a lease immediately before dispatch, the number that matters is not average throughput but whether the single publish at the critical moment can fail, and with no retry at all it can. Limitation: real readers are bursty rather than tight-looping, so the deployed collision rate is far below 88%; this experiment bounds the shape of the problem, not its production frequency, and I did not measure interference from Defender specifically.

nodes.title: A real ledger holds 6 duplicate seq values written 1.4 s apart by two live writers
nodes.body: In `C:/Users/Darkness/.dsh/loom/campaigns/loom-self3/events.jsonl` seq 30 through 35 each appear twice: seq 30 is `round.finished {n:3,status:interrupted,reason:host-restart}` at t=1793990305168 and `attempt.finished {id:"r3a2"}` at t=1793990306529; seq 31 is `candidate.proposed r3a1` and `round.started {n:4}` at t=1793990306619; the same pattern repeats to 35. Across 69 campaign ledgers this is 6 events, all in that one file, all within 1.4 seconds. Here the mechanism is in `src/core/ledger.js:31-36`: append calls #sync(), which compares only file *size*, then computes `this.seq + 1` from its own in-memory copy; two writers that both saw the same size both compute the same next seq and both appends land. Size is a weak watermark: two events of equal byte length are indistinguishable from no change at all. Limitation: this is a two-writer fault, and with the ownership lock actually holding there is one writer, so the trigger is the ownership and recovery defects below rather than normal steady-state running; one file out of 69 also means the rate is low, not that the class is rare.

nodes.title: normalize keeps the first event per seq, deleting 3 attempt.finished and a round.started
nodes.body: `src/core/ledger.js:60-73` keeps the first event it meets for a seq and drops the rest. On loom-self3 that deletes 3 `attempt.finished`, 2 `lesson.impact` and 1 `round.started`: the surviving fold has round 4 `finished` with no `round.started` at all (an orphan round), and r3a2's attempt result disappears while the round-3 `interrupted` closure survives. Here the mechanism is that the dedupe rule treats a duplicate seq as a duplicated *write*, when this pair is two different facts; the reader cannot tell, so it resolves by position in the file, which is not the order the facts were decided. Why this is worse than it looks: the dropped events are exactly the ones a restart reconciler needs, so the repair path destroys the evidence it was written to consume. Limitation: dropping is better than folding the same round twice, which would corrupt every derived number, so this is a choice between two wrong answers and the comment in the code says so; the real fix is a writer identity that makes duplicates impossible, not a smarter dedupe.

nodes.title: Leases record no pid, host or fencing token, so any boot declares a live attempt abandoned
nodes.body: writeLease (`src/runtime/lease.js:18-33`) stores attemptId, round, sessionId, startedAt, deadline, lastSeq, lastAdvanceAt, state, reason: no pid, no host identity, no monotonic token. reconcileLeases (`src/runtime/lease.js:80-92`) marks every `running` lease `abandoned` with reason `host-restart`, unconditionally. In loom-self4 the ledger shows `attempt.abandoned r4a1 host-restart` at t=1793993377902 and `round.finished n:4 interrupted` at t=1793993377905, then r4a1 finishing at 1793993397179 and r4a2 at 1793993397878, and round 4 closing `no-gain` at 1793993397889 — recovery ran against a round that was still alive. Here the mechanism is that "running" is unscoped: the booting process has no way to ask whether the owner still exists, so presence of the record is treated as proof of death. This is the classic case for fencing tokens, and the reason Kleppmann's lease critique applies: a lease grants no exclusivity unless the resource it guards rejects the old token, and here the resource is an append-only log that accepts any writer. Limitation: the sequence is also consistent with a real host death whose child agents survived as orphaned OS processes, which is arguably the correct thing to abandon; the ledger alone cannot distinguish the two.

nodes.title: Boot claims loop ownership unconditionally, so a hot reload steals the loop from a live owner
nodes.body: claimOwnership (`src/core/lock.js:38-46`) reads the previous record, writes its own, and returns `{ok:true, previous}` without ever refusing; `src/index.js:78` calls it on every plugin apply. The tick path is careful by contrast: ensureOwner (`src/runtime/runtime.js:361-382`) takes over only when `!state.owner || !state.alive || !state.fresh`, which is the correct rule. apply.log shows one process (pid 26448) applying 5 times in an evening with instance ids 4de39cc3, 669e117b, d4810987, d687c491, 0085c33e — five claims, five new owners, no refusal. Here the mechanism is that newest-writer-wins was chosen so a restart is never blocked by a dead pid lock, but the same rule lets an in-process reload start a second scheduler while the first one's round is still in flight, producing exactly the two-writer condition that corrupted seq in loom-self3. Why the two paths disagree: the boot path asks "am I allowed to run" and answers yes, the tick path asks "is anyone else running" and checks. Limitation: the old runtime is disposed by its effect cleanup (`src/index.js:167`) before the new claim in the normal reload order, so the overlap window is the dispose ordering, which I did not measure; dispatcher dispose is fire-and-forget (`Promise.resolve(d.dispose())`), so it may still be cancelling children when the new owner ticks.

nodes.title: Workspace repair is fire-and-forget while the first tick runs 250 ms later
nodes.body: In runtime.recover() (`src/runtime/runtime.js:518-535`) repairWorkspace is launched with a `.then(...)` and never awaited, while `src/index.js:160-162` schedules `setTimeout(tick, 250)`. The repair runs `git checkout -- .` (`src/exec/worktree.js:330-333`) and `rmSync` of patch-created paths (`src/runtime/recovery.js:119-129`) inside the campaign workspace — the same tree the next round inspects with `git status` and diffs against HEAD. No lock is taken between repair and dispatch, so the round can observe a half-restored tree, conclude it is dirty, and refuse to apply (`workspace-dirty` in `src/exec/patch.js:66-68`), or diff against a base that is about to change. Here the mechanism is that the comment justifies the async launch as keeping tools usable on boot, which is a real requirement, but the same asynchrony also removes the only barrier between a destructive repair and the first reader. Limitation: the repair only runs when there is an unproven landing, which is rare, and both git commands are fast, so the window is narrow; I have not observed a round corrupted by it, only the code path that permits it.

nodes.title: Re-approving a committed checkpoint writes committed:false, then recovery withdraws the landing
nodes.body: The approve branch of rsi_decide (`src/tools/index.js:678-745`) applies the patch, runs the guard, commits, appends `autopilot.applied {committed, commit}`, and only then appends `checkpoint.answered`. A crash between the commit and the answered append leaves the checkpoint open. Answering it again reaches applyPatch's reverse-check (`git apply --reverse --check`, `src/exec/patch.js:62-66`), which returns `{ok:true, reason:'already-applied'}`, and then commitWorkspace finds nothing to commit and returns `{committed:false, sha:null}` (`src/exec/worktree.js:362-380`), so the second `autopilot.applied` claims committed:false. unprovenLandings (`src/runtime/recovery.js:56-80`) then emits `round.unlanded` and repairWorkspace restores tracked files and deletes patch-created files, undoing a change that was committed and human-approved. Here the mechanism is that the proof of landing is a field on an event that a legitimate retry cannot reproduce, so "not provable from this event" is conflated with "not landed". Limitation: I found no instance in 69 real ledgers; 5 rounds are promoted-but-landed:false, but `git apply --reverse --check` fails on their patches, meaning those landings genuinely did not happen, so this remains a code-path finding rather than an observed incident.

nodes.title: Host death orphans the verifier shell: taskkill fires only on timeout, no Job Object ties it
nodes.body: runVerifier (`src/exec/verifier.js`) spawns with `shell: true` and calls terminateTree only when the deadline expires or the attempt is aborted; nothing binds the spawned tree to the host process. The child agent is a session inside the host, so it dies with the host, but the verifier is a separate cmd.exe tree that keeps running, still holding handles in the worktree and still writing whatever output files the command writes. Here the mechanism is that Windows has no signal-based process-group kill and no parent-death inheritance that reaches grandchildren; a Job Object with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE is the only stock mechanism and it is not in use here. Why this is an exactly-once problem and not a tidiness problem: after a restart the campaign can re-run the same attempt while the old verifier is still mutating the same worktree, so the side effect happens twice with no ledger event either time — at-least-once delivery of a command that author believed ran once. Limitation: a verifier is supposed to be read-only with respect to the campaign workspace, so in the common case the duplicate costs CPU and port contention rather than corruption; it becomes corruption only for commands that write artifacts or hit external services.

nodes.title: night-committer.mjs commits any dirty tree every 20 s with no lease, guarded by two status calls
nodes.body: The script runs the full suite (up to 600 s), then `git add -A && git commit` in the repo root; its only defence against catching a half-applied patch is `git status --porcelain` taken twice with a 1.5 s gap plus countOpenGates before and after the suite (the gap is a `spawnSync(process.execPath, ['-e','setTimeout(()=>{},1500)'])`). It coordinates with the loop through no lock and no lease. Here the mechanism is specific: the loop's own invariant is that a landing counts only once committed, and a different process committing the dirty tree inside the apply-to-commit window makes git true while the ledger still records `committed:false`, which is precisely the state recovery reads to withdraw the landing and restore the tree. A status that is stable for 1.5 s proves the apply has not started, not that it has finished. Limitation: the script never reverts and checks gates twice, so the realistic damage is committing unverified work rather than losing it; night.log shows 6 `commit failed:` lines with empty stderr and 5 successes, but nothing that proves a half-applied patch was committed.

nodes.title: Crash-only design fits this loop but shifts the whole burden onto idempotent recovery
nodes.body: Candea and Fox (HotOS 2003) argue that the only way to stop software should be to crash it and the only way to start it should be recovery, which deletes the rarely exercised clean-shutdown path. loom is crash-only in exactly this sense: dispose aborts children, boot runs recover() before ticking, and every repair is expressed as new ledger events rather than an edit. Why this works: the mechanism is that recovery must be a total function of the durable log, so running it twice is a no-op; `tests/chaos2/recover-idempotent.test.mjs` asserts precisely that (second recovery appends nothing). What crash-only does not supply is exclusivity or ownership: it silently assumes one recoverer and one log writer, which is the assumption nodes on duplicate seq, lease fencing and boot-time lock stealing show is unenforced here. Why the original setting is easier: the paper's systems sit behind middleware that absorbs retries, so a duplicate recovery is hidden from users; a workstation loop has no such layer, so the same design carries more risk in this context than in its own. Limitation: the paper is a position paper with no measurements, and its central claim (faster recovery, less code) is not falsifiable from it; I could not find a study that measures crash-only versus clean-shutdown failure rates in practice.

nodes.title: A job killed at 70% sent the monthly statement to 40,000 customers twice
nodes.body: The job read every account, rendered a PDF and called the email provider for each customer in turn, keeping the list of statements already sent only in memory. At roughly 70% it reached its 2 GB memory limit, the kernel killed the container (exit 137), the pod was marked failed and the replacement pod began again at the first customer. About forty thousand customers received the statement twice and a few thousand three times. Here the mechanism is the one loom's attempt model reproduces exactly: progress that lives only inside the running process is invisible to whatever restarts it, so the restart replays effects that already happened, and the replay is indistinguishable from the original work because nothing outside the process recorded either. The repair the author draws is not a retry limit but an addressable effect — one durable record per customer, written before the send, so that replay becomes a no-op. Limitation: this is a first-person engineering blog post without a company-verified postmortem, so the 40,000 figure is the author's own; and the failure was triggered by memory pressure, not by lease expiry, so it is evidence for the general shape of duplicate side effects rather than for any specific mechanism in loom.

nodes.title: Nobody has randomised checkpoint cadence in an agent supervision loop
nodes.body: Every batching result we have comes from another channel: smartphone notifications (Fitz 2019), email and IM scheduling (Iqbal and Bailey 2008), clinical advisories (Ancker 2017). Not one of them randomised streaming against a digest for human approval of machine work, and none measured the two things our design turns on: whether a delayed checkpoint loses the information needed to decide it, and how much an urgent exception costs when it waits for the window. Why it matters: our batching argument is an import from a domain where the item is a notification and the risk of delay is a missed message rather than a missed irreversible apply. What would settle it: one loop, one task family, three arms (stream, three-times-daily digest, one daily digest), measuring decision latency, catch rate against seeded known-bad candidates, and reviewer strain over at least two weeks to get past novelty.

nodes.title: No measurement of time-to-decision or error rate for an evidence-dense card against a raw diff
nodes.body: We could not find a single study that puts an evidence-dense decision summary and a raw diff side by side and measures seconds to a decision, agreement with a ground-truth verdict, or confidence calibration. The nearest numbers are clinical (a median 8 seconds to process a drug-interaction alert) and code review (position bias, silent approval rates), and neither isolates the presentation format. Why it matters: evidence-dense decisions is our central interface bet, and the only mechanism evidence we have cuts against it, since reviewers decide against a pre-formed expectation and added density doubled mental demand in the Sidecar study. What would settle it: a within-subjects study on real candidate diffs with a known-bad seed and three formats (diff only, diff plus verifier output, diff plus a card with the falsifying evidence first), measuring time-to-decision and false-accept rate.

nodes.title: No published figure exists for how often a human opens a dashboard that is available to them
nodes.body: The metric is technically collectable, since Grafana Enterprise and Cloud store dashboard views both aggregated and per user over a trailing window, and practitioners clearly scrape it to decide what to delete. But the only numbers we found are unsourced: one blog claims 41 of 340 dashboards had a view in thirty days, about 12%, and a forum audit claims 80% of stored telemetry was never accessed in sixty days, neither with a stated sample frame or method. Why it matters: if a loop exposes a dashboard and counts that as supervision, the open rate is the denominator of every oversight claim we make, and we currently have no defensible value for it. What would settle it: instrument our own loop, publish views per available surface per week alongside decisions taken, and report the share of surfaces with zero views, since that is the number that says whether a surface is supervision or decoration.

nodes.title: No data on whether a repeated decision card's approval rate decays the way repeated clinical alerts do
nodes.body: Clinical data says repeats are the poison: 30% lower acceptance per extra item and 10% per five points of repeat share, with first-instance override locking in 87.9% of later overrides. Agent-loop cards are structurally repeat-prone, since the same unspecified fork recurs every run, and one design argument holds that the card should therefore be answered once and written into the standing brief. But nobody has measured a card's acceptance curve over repetitions, so we cannot say whether the tenth appearance of the same card is ignored at the clinical rate, is still read because the surrounding diff changed, or is actively harmful because it crowds out the new item. Why it matters: our cadence and card design both depend on which of those is true. What would settle it: log card identity across runs in one loop and report acceptance by appearance index for the same card.

nodes.title: Every effect size here was measured with a gold-test harness; ours is a shell command of unknown precision
nodes.body: All the numbers above are computed against a benchmark harness whose tests are known to be correct, and the one paper that varies verifier quality directly shows the answer moving by 14pp. Our verifier is a shell command and an exit code, unmeasured for precision, so every effect size in this file is an upper bound on what we could reproduce, and an effect that is real in the repo may be undetectable through our instrument. The cheap fix that makes the rest of this list usable is a mutation audit: mutate the source in ways the tests should catch, run the verifier, and keep the fraction that still exits 0. That runs without a model, is deterministic, and converts the promotion gate from a coin with an opinion into a measurement. Until it exists, comparing cheap wins is comparing noise to noise.

nodes.title: Nobody has ablated per-attempt lesson injection; the nearest measurements are a null static file and a strong
nodes.body: The literature brackets our lesson mechanism from both sides without testing it. On one side, a 288-run ablation of static context files found no correctness effect. On the other, a harness study found raw trace access lifted accuracy to 50.0 from 34.6 with scores alone, while LLM-written summaries added nothing over scores. A one-sentence claim written after a specific failure is neither of those: it is not static, and it is not a summary of the whole trajectory. I could not find a study that ablates it, so the 2.6pp test-writing null and the context-file null are suggestive rather than decisive, and our own loop is one of the few places the measurement could be made cheaply, since we already record per-attempt outcomes and already inject the claims.

nodes.title: None of these effect sizes are normalised by human attention, which is the axis the loop actually optimises
nodes.body: Every cost denominator in this file is dollars, tokens or wall-clock. None is human minutes, and several levers that look free on a token budget are not free on an attention budget: more retries produce more candidate patches to triage, model routing produces more failure modes to explain, and a verifier change produces different checkpoints. If attention is the scarce resource, a lever with a 2pp token win and a 1.5x checkpoint count is a loss. The measurement is easy to specify and absent from the literature: human minutes per landed promotion, recorded next to tokens per landed promotion, both divided by the same denominator so the two cannot be traded silently.

nodes.title: Revert-on-failure is studied only as patch selection, never as rollback, so its effect is unmeasured
nodes.body: The closest measured thing is best-of-N with an oracle verifier, which is selection among candidates that all exist, not rollback of one candidate on a dirty tree. Nothing I found isolates the rollback policy itself: how much a `git checkout` between attempts changes the next attempt's success rate, as distinct from the retry budget it consumes. The mechanism that makes it plausibly large is that a failed attempt leaves edited files that the next attempt reads as ground truth, so not reverting can propagate a wrong premise; the mechanism that makes it plausibly small is that agents mostly rewrite the same regions anyway. It is cheap to test in our own loop because the worktree already exists, which makes this a gap we can close rather than one we must cite.

nodes.title: The core premise has no head-to-head test; a within-task randomised design is buildable and cheap at our scale
nodes.body: Nothing in the literature attempts the four-arm comparison the premise requires: autonomous loop, autonomous loop plus batched checkpoint review, interactive human-driven session, and human alone, on the same task set with matched wall-clock and token budget. A defensible design exists at our scale: take 20-30 tasks, randomise each task to regime, run k>=5 seeds per cell to beat the 1.5pp SD floor, and pre-register the primary metric as cost-per-accepted-change rather than pass rate, because interactive regimes win trivially on pass rate when a human supplies the missing requirement. The confound to name up front is that the interactive arm gets more human minutes, so the honest comparison is at equal total cost, not equal task count.

nodes.title: Nobody measures the marginal value of an agent approval gate; seeded known-bad checkpoints would make it measu
nodes.body: The MAP survey found 74% of deployed agent systems rely on human verification and none compared outcomes with and without it, and no published work reports a detection rate for a real agent approval queue. The cheap instrument is a seeded-defect probe: inject a small fraction of previously accepted but known-bad changes into the checkpoint queue, unannounced, and record the catch rate, the time-to-decision and the approval rate on clean items. This converts the gate from an unexamined ritual into a measurable instrument with a false-negative rate, and it is the only design I found that can distinguish rubber-stamping from correct filtering - the ambiguity that makes both the 95% approval figure and the clinical override-rate literature uninterpretable.

nodes.title: There is no evidence on whether batched, asynchronous checkpoint review is worse than synchronous review - the
nodes.body: Our design batches checkpoints so the human reviews several L0/L1 outcomes at once, which is a deliberate choice with no direct evidence behind it. Every habituation study I found delivers prompts synchronously and in sequence; batching changes the unit of judgement, the delay before feedback, and the amount of state the reviewer must reconstruct, and it could plausibly help (fewer context switches, comparative judgement within a batch) or hurt (later feedback arrives after the loop has already committed downstream work). The discriminating experiment is straightforward: same checkpoint content, same reviewer pool, batched versus per-item delivery, measuring catch rate on seeded defects and the rate at which reversals are still cheap to apply. Until that runs, the batching decision is an aesthetic preference.

nodes.title: No measured decay curve for a holdout the worker can read
nodes.body: Kumar's sqrt(2 ln k / n) is derived for i.i.d. examples and independent configurations, and our corpus has one holdout id, no saturated campaign, and no counterfactual where the same tasks were graded blind. So how many rounds a holdout stays informative in a repo-readable agentic loop is unknown rather than merely unmeasured here. The measurement that would settle it: freeze a task set, run N rounds with the holdout readable and N with it served from outside the workspace, and plot gate agreement between the two arms against round index; decay shows up as the two arms diverging after some k.

nodes.title: No contamination detector that works when the graded system can read the eval set
nodes.body: All five published detection families infer contamination from a trace that presupposes bounded access; none detects 'the candidate opened the file it is graded by'. The only family that survives is re-collection or date-slicing, which costs task authoring rather than compute. A candidate detector that fits loom: record every filesystem read the worker session makes and flag any read under the campaign directory or of a path appearing in an eval task's verify command — cheap, auditable, and independent of what the model claims.

nodes.title: The rotation trigger and its cost are unmeasured for agentic loops
nodes.body: Bernstein implements a 0.90-over-3-submissions saturation trigger with no published before/after, and the literature offers reuse counts, information budgets and date slices as alternatives with no comparison in this setting. Open: how many fresh holdout items per promotion is affordable, whether a saturation trigger fires before or after the set stops discriminating, and whether rotating mid-campaign makes round-to-round scores incomparable — which would break the `beatsIncumbent` comparison that the whole gate rests on.

nodes.title: The task prompt itself states the acceptance content, a leak channel upstream of the holdout
nodes.body: loom-life registers tasks whose prompts literally quote the assertions to satisfy, so the acceptance content is in the brief before any repository read happens. Whether a holdout can be meaningful when the held-in task already states its assertions is unmeasured, and it is a distinct channel from repository readability: even a perfectly access-controlled holdout cannot help if the work task hands the worker the acceptance text. The cheap test: regrade the same patches with prompts rewritten to state the goal but not the assertions, and compare pass rates.

nodes.title: No study measures minutes for a code-review decision on an agent-produced diff with a machine verifier already
nodes.body: Every number found is either human-authored code (di Biase 13-14 min, Google 24-line medians, Meta TimeSpent) or a security finding with a tool explanation (SAFE 3.5 min), and none measures the exact loom surface: a diff from an agent, a shell verifier already green or red, and a paired baseline showing the previous score. The nearest published attempt to test evidence packaging for peer review, 'Evaluating the Effects of Automated Test Results, Model Solutions, and Checklists on Peer Code Review: A Quantitative Study' (ACM, 11 Nov 2026, doi 10.1145/3795867.3830991), is unreachable: dl.acm.org returns a Cloudflare 403 to both fetch engines, so only its title and acceptance metadata are known. The measurement that would settle it is a within-subject crossover with timestamped open-to-verdict intervals over at least ~30 decisions per arm, since the observed per-decision spread (4.7 vs 5.1 min, p=.21 at n=24) means anything smaller is unfalsifiable.

nodes.title: The review-cost literature repeatedly concludes more than its own time data shows, which is what we would be d
nodes.body: di Biase et al. measured no time or defect benefit from decomposition yet concluded commits should be separated as best practice; SmartBear's 200-400 LOC ceiling is a 2006 vendor case study without a control group whose own PDF is no longer fetchable; Getty reports a process change and a bug found but no minutes; LinearB's queue numbers come from an undisclosed vendor pipeline. This pattern is the strongest counter-evidence to confidence in any single denominator constant: the field's canonical numbers are either uncontrolled or no longer verifiable. The measurement that would break the pattern for loom is a published per-checkpoint log, including rejected checkpoints and the minutes spent before each rejection, so an outside reader can recompute the denominator rather than trust a summary. No such log exists for any agent loop we could find.

nodes.title: Unknown whether the 3.5-minute decision constant survives contact with real diffs, or is an artefact of lab tr
nodes.body: The SAFE study's median 3.5 minutes per finding comes from 24 participants in a lab, on security findings from the OWASP Benchmark with injected material, in 15-minute blocks, with time reconstructed from transcripts rather than instrumented, and its participants reached only two or three of five findings. di Biase's 13-14 minutes comes from one small Java system with a convenience sample. Both are plausible and neither transfers: the deployment surface for loom is a maintainer looking at a diff they did not write on a codebase they know well, which the literature suggests is the cheap case (comprehension is where the 58% of time goes, and familiarity is the main input to it), but no study isolates familiarity as a moderator of decision time. The falsifying measurement is a field sample of checkpoint decisions on one real repository with per-decision timestamps, stratified by whether the reviewer had previously touched the affected files.

nodes.title: Nobody has tested what a fencing token would actually change on this loop
nodes.body: Adding hostId and a monotonic epoch to lease records is cheap, but the only resource that could reject a stale token is the ledger, and it currently accepts any writer. The experiment is to record the epoch in every appended event and have normalize drop events whose epoch is below the highest seen for that attempt, then replay the loom-self4 timeline to see whether the r4a1/r4a2 finishes would have been admitted or silently dropped. Until that is run, the fencing-token argument is a plausible analogy from distributed systems, not a demonstrated improvement — and the failure mode of the naive version is precisely the silent data loss already measured in normalize.

nodes.title: No crash-injection test exists for power loss, and the fsync defect is therefore unmeasured
nodes.body: The missing fsync in writeJsonAtomic and the missing directory flush cannot be demonstrated by killing a process, because the OS still has the pages; they need a VM-level power cut or a filesystem that reorders. loom has three chaos suites that kill processes and none that cut power, so the durability half of restart safety has never been exercised. The concrete test: run N publishes in a VM, cut power at a random instant, and count how many of the corresponding files come back truncated or zero-length. Without it, the claim that state files are crash-safe is an assumption inherited from POSIX folklore applied to NTFS.

nodes.title: No duplicated side effect has ever been observed in 69 real campaign ledgers — the risk is untested, not dispr
nodes.body: I searched all 69 ledgers for duplicate checkpoint answers, duplicate autopilot.applied for one round, and repeated attempt ids; the only duplication found was at the event-seq level, not at the effect level. That is weak evidence either way: the loop's effects so far are mostly patches into a git worktree, where re-applying is content-checked and therefore naturally idempotent (`already-applied` in applyPatch). The genuinely non-idempotent effects — sending a notification, raising a checkpoint a human sees twice, spending money on a duplicate child session — are not in the ledger at all, so their absence proves nothing. A negative result from a ledger that cannot record the effect is not evidence of safety.

nodes.title: Defender interference is asserted by every source and measured by none of them here
nodes.body: Both the claude-hooks and gortex fixes cite antivirus and search indexers as the cause of transient EPERM, and Microsoft's own docs on ReplaceFile document failure codes that leave the destination missing. But none of the sources give a rate, and my measurement used synthetic tight-loop readers rather than a real scanner. The missing experiment is to publish the same file once per second for an hour on a machine with Defender real-time protection on, and count failures; that number decides whether this is a one-in-a-thousand annoyance or the dominant cause of lost leases. Until it exists, the design choice between retry, append-only leases, and open-with-FILE_SHARE_DELETE rests on an analogy.
